notes:
Here is the verse-by-verse commentary on Leviticus 18, drawn exclusively from the sources I was able to access.

---

## Leviticus 18 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

### Overview / Structure

The chapter falls into two major parts: vv. 1–23 give the prohibitions (the "what not to do"), and vv. 24–30 give the reasons (the "why not to do it"). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_18_commentary)

Matthew Henry divides it as: (I) a general law against conformity to the corrupt usages of the heathen (vv. 1–5); (II) particular laws against incest (vv. 6–18) and against "beastly lusts and barbarous idolatries" (vv. 19–23); (III) the enforcement from the ruin of the Canaanites (vv. 24–30). (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/18.htm)

Keil & Delitzsch call the chapter "Holiness of the Marriage Relation." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

---

### v. 1: "Then the LORD said to Moses"

**Ellicott** notes that, unlike preceding communications dealing with ritual and ceremonial pollutions, this one treats moral life — "precepts which form the basis of domestic purity, and which are the foundation of human happiness." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Enduring Word (Guzik)** says this chapter is "one of the most extensive and direct passages in the Bible reflecting God's stated will and commands regarding the expression of human sexuality." These are God's words, and therefore carry "immeasurably more authority than the words, opinions, theories, desires, feelings, longings, or wishes of any person or persons." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-18/)

---

### v. 2: "I am the LORD your God"

**Ellicott**: The phrase establishes that the Lord is Israel's "recognised and sole sovereign." They are bound to obey His precepts and not the customs of the nations around them. The phrase is repeated emphatically in vv. 4 and 30. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch**: This phrase, placed at the head and repeated at the close (v. 30), enforces obedience "upon the people as a covenant obligation." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

**Precept Austin**: "It all begins with God, the great 'I Am.' He is reminding them of the fact that He is their covenant keeping God." This phrase occurs 49 times in Leviticus out of 161 times in the entire OT. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_18_commentary)

**Guzik**: Before giving a single command, God laid a foundation: "You belong to Me; you shall not do as the world does." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-18/)

---

### v. 3: "You must not follow the practices of the land of Egypt…or…Canaan"

**Ellicott**: The Israelites had become familiar with Egyptian practices during their sojourn, and the danger was increased by the fact that "these licentious practices obtained in worse forms in the land which they were to inherit." It is a warning against both the past (Egypt) and the future (Canaan). "Neither shall ye walk in their ordinances" condemns even acts that were "legalised" in those cultures. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Guzik**: This is the principle of non-conformity to the world. "In many ways, the modern western world is moving further and further from a Biblically guided sexual morality." Christians must "not do according to the doings of the surrounding culture." Rooker is quoted noting that "seven times in the introduction and conclusion the Israelites are commanded not to act as the other nations." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-18/)

**Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics)**: This verse teaches that "the highest civilization is no sufficient reason for a certain line of conduct" (Egypt was the pinnacle of civilization) and "prevailing custom is no sufficient reason" either. Worldly conformity is "simian imitation." Conformity to prevailing custom "costs nothing, except indeed the sacrifice of principle." (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/leviticus/18.htm)

**Precept Austin**: God had redeemed them from Egyptian bondage, but "He had not gotten Egypt out of them." Forewarned is forearmed. The pagan "statutes" must have "legalised" practices God considered detestable. Extra-biblical writings attest to the "sex saturated" society of idol-worshipping pagans with their fertility cults. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_18_commentary)

---

### v. 4: "You are to practice My judgments and keep My statutes"

**Ellicott**: The expression "My judgments and Mine ordinances" is emphatic, in opposition to "their ordinances," and carries the force of "Mine only" — as Christ explained "Him shalt thou serve" (Deut 6:13) as "Him only shalt thou serve" (Matt 4:10). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Precept Austin**: God never asks anything of us that He does not also enable us to obey. The phrase "I am the LORD your God" is linked to His name JEHOVAH M'KADDESH ("the LORD who sanctifies you"). Israel had the responsibility to choose obedience; God was the one who provided the sanctifying power. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_18_commentary)

---

### v. 5: "Keep My statutes…for the man who does these things will live by them"

**Ellicott**: "He shall live by or through them" — by observing them, the law-abiding will live a happy and prosperous life, since disobedience exposes the offender to death. The spiritual authorities in the time of the second Temple interpreted this to mean "shall have life eternal." Paul quotes this passage in Romans 10:5 and Galatians 3:12, contrasting this promise made to works with the promise of the Gospel made to faith. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch**: "The man who does them shall live (gain true life) through them." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

**Precept Austin (citing Wiersbe and MacArthur)**: This was "a way of life, not a way of salvation." It was the way of life for the redeemed, not a way of salvation for the lost. MacArthur notes that the verse promises temporal blessings for obedience, but also has a "higher reference to spiritual life." Wiersbe says: "If people could perfectly obey God's law, their obedience would save them, but, of course, nobody can. Therefore, salvation is wholly by faith, totally apart from the works of the law." Everett's Study Notes add that if a man breaks just one law, "he becomes guilty before God as if he had broken all" (James 2:10). (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_18_commentary)

**Guzik**: This verse shows God's laws are designed to build the best life. "If a man does, he shall live by them; if he does not, he may die by them." The sickness and disease associated with sexual immorality is "only one obvious way that disobedience to God's wisdom takes away from life." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-18/)

---

### v. 6: "None of you are to approach any close relative to have sexual relations"

**Ellicott**: The Hebrew literally reads "man, man, ye shall not approach" — a phrase intended to mean "no man whatsoever shall approach." The absence of "of the house of Israel" shows these prohibitions also bind "the stranger who took up his abode among the Israelites." The phrase "near of kin" (literally "flesh of his flesh") covers kinship of both consanguinity and affinity. Ellicott also discusses the debate over whether "uncover nakedness" refers to illicit commerce or incestuous marriage, concluding that it denotes sexual intercourse both within and without matrimony. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch**: "Flesh of his flesh" means belonging to the same flesh as oneself (Genesis 2:24) — applied to blood-relationship. The prohibition relates to both married and unmarried intercourse, "though the reference is chiefly to the former." Notably, Keil observes that sexual intercourse with a daughter is not expressly mentioned, "simply because the crime was regarded as one that never could occur" — as parricide is not mentioned in Exodus 21:15. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

**Guzik**: The very first command shows that God's standard rises above physical pleasure. "God never intended that the pursuit of physical pleasure be the highest purpose and good of the sexual act." The phrase "uncover nakedness" is broad enough to include inappropriate activity short of intercourse (such as oral sex, molestation, and pornography). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-18/)

**Precept Austin (William MacDonald)**: This is the general principle: "Marriage with a blood relative was forbidden." Modern medicine confirms that in marriages of blood relatives, "the physical or mental weaknesses of parents tend to be magnified in the children." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_18_commentary)

---

### v. 7: "You must not expose the nakedness of your father by having sexual relations with your mother"

**Ellicott**: The Authorised Version rendering is based on the interpretation that this injunction is addressed to both daughter and son — the daughter must not have relations with the father, nor the son with the mother (citing the case of Lot's daughters, Genesis 19:31–38). Alternatively, it can be translated literally: "the nakedness of thy father, and the nakedness of thy mother shalt thou not uncover," because they being one flesh, the nakedness of one is the nakedness of the other. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch**: Sexual connection with a mother is called "uncovering the nakedness of father and mother." As husband and wife are one flesh (Genesis 2:24), "the nakedness of the husband is uncovered in that of his wife." Keil disagrees with the interpretation that this refers to a daughter-father relationship, arguing that "all these laws are intended for the man alone, and addressed expressly to him." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

**Matthew Henry**: These laws "are consonant to the very light and law of nature." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/18.htm)

---

### v. 8: "You must not have sexual relations with your father's wife"

**Ellicott**: This law is directed against illicit commerce with a stepmother. The administrators of the law during the second Temple defined it as: a man's father's wife is forever prohibited, whether betrothed, married, divorced, or widowed. If he lies with her while her husband is alive, he is doubly guilty — because she is near of kin and because she is another man's wife. This includes the sin of Reuben with Bilhah (Genesis 35:22) and Absalom with his father's wives (2 Samuel 16:20–23). Among the ancient Arabs, marriages with stepmothers were common; the Koran (Sura 4:27), like the Mosaic law, proscribes them. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch**: Intercourse with a father's wife is forbidden as "uncovering the father's nakedness." "By the 'father's wife' we are probably to understand not merely his full lawful wife, but his concubine also." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

**Guzik**: Sex among people in these relationships is condemned even if both are consenting adults. The case in 1 Corinthians 5:1 (a man with his stepmother) is cited as an example. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-18/)

---

### v. 9: "You must not have sexual relations with your sister"

**Ellicott**: Though Abraham married his half-sister (Genesis 20:12), and Athenians and Spartans permitted marriages with half-sisters, this law is explicit. Yet the narrative of Amnon and Tamar shows the practice continued in spite of the law. The phrase "born at home or elsewhere" refers to whether the sister was born in wedlock or was illegitimate (per the second Temple authorities). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch**: By "sister, the daughter of father or mother," we are to understand the half-sister. The clause "whether born at home or born abroad" does not refer to legitimate vs. illegitimate birth, but refers to the half-sister "of the first marriage, whether the father's daughter left by a deceased wife, or the mother's daughter left by a deceased husband." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

---

### v. 10: "You must not have sexual relations with your son's daughter or your daughter's daughter"

**Ellicott**: From this prohibition it is inferred that a man must not marry his own daughter — if a granddaughter is proscribed, "how much more his own daughter." Ellicott suggests it is "more than probable that a word has dropped out of the text" and that originally it included "the nakedness of thy daughter." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch**: The prohibition is explained by the words "for they are thy nakedness" — because they were directly descended from the grandfather, "carnal intercourse with them would be equivalent to dishonouring his own flesh and blood." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

---

### v. 11: "You must not have sexual relations with the daughter of your father's wife, born to your father"

**Ellicott**: If this clause stood alone, it would denote a stepmother's daughter by a previous husband — no blood relation at all. But "begotten by thy father" shows she is a half-sister on the father's side. To avoid "a senseless repetition" of v. 9, Ellicott suggests either regarding this as a marginal gloss that crept into the text, or correcting the first letter of the disjunctive particle in v. 9 so that v. 9 prohibits a full sister and v. 11 a half-sister. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch**: This is the half-sister by a second marriage, and the prohibition refers to "the son by a first marriage, whereas v. 9 treats of the son by a second marriage." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

---

### vv. 12–13: Father's sister and mother's sister (aunts)

**Ellicott**: Remarkably, Moses himself was the offspring of such an alliance — Amram married his own aunt Jochebed (Exodus 6:20). The second Temple authorities understood the prohibition strictly to apply between nephews and aunts but not vice versa (uncles and nieces). They regarded intermarriage between uncle and niece as "an especially meritorious act," and this is illustrated by Nahor marrying Milcah (his brother's daughter, Genesis 11:29) and Othniel marrying Achsah (his niece, Joshua 15:17). Among Jews to this day, intermarriages between uncles and nieces are of common occurrence. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch**: Marriage with either the paternal or maternal aunt was prohibited "because she was the blood-relation of the father or mother." The penalty was not death by the magistrate but that the offenders would "bear their iniquity" or die childless — a punishment from God Himself. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

---

### v. 14: Father's brother's wife (uncle's wife)

**Ellicott**: A nephew is to have no commerce with her during her husband's lifetime, nor marry her when his uncle is dead. Transgressors were doomed to die without issue (Leviticus 20:20). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

---

### v. 15: Daughter-in-law

**Ellicott**: The second Temple legislators defined this prohibition as applicable even when the daughter-in-law had only been espoused, or after she was divorced or widowed. Both parties were punished with death (Leviticus 20:12). The Koran (4:27) similarly regards such alliances with abhorrence. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch**: This is called *tebel* (confusion) in Leviticus 20:12 — "a sinful mixing up or confusing of the divine ordinances by unnatural unchastity." Punishable by death for both parties. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

---

### v. 16: Brother's wife

**Ellicott**: Though alliance with a brother's wife is forbidden here, the law is not absolute. Under the Levirate law (Deuteronomy 25:5), if a brother died without issue, it became a "moral and civil duty" for the surviving brother to marry the widow. This shows the prohibition could not be based on incest, "since that which is inherently incestuous the Divine law itself would under no circumstances have set aside." Ellicott recounts a striking Talmudic story of a man required to marry twelve widows of his brothers. To this day, orthodox Jews still observe this law. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch**: The prohibition "only refers to cases in which the deceased brother had left children; for if he had died childless, the brother not only might, but was required to marry his sister-in-law." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

**Matthew Henry**: The exception was "peculiar to the Jewish state" and "now that those reasons have ceased the exception ceases, and the law is in force." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/18.htm)

---

### v. 17: "You must not have sexual relations with both a woman and her daughter"

**Ellicott**: If a man marries a widow who has a daughter, or forms an alliance with a woman who has a daughter out of wedlock, he is forbidden also to marry the daughter. This also covers the granddaughter. For contracting this kind of polygamy, offenders were punished with death by fire (Leviticus 20:14). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch**: This is described in Deuteronomy 27:20 as "an accursed lying with the mother-in-law." Both were crimes of *zimmah* (wickedness / licentiousness) punishable by death for both parties. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

**Guzik**: The term "wickedness" (*zimmah*) is "a very general one…used to describe any kind of morally unacceptable or detestable action." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-18/)

---

### v. 18: "You must not take your wife's sister as a rival wife"

**Ellicott** devotes the longest discussion to this verse. The marginal rendering in some Bibles ("one wife to another," making this a prohibition of all polygamy) is rejected for several reasons: (1) "wife" and "sister" consistently mean wife and sister in these prohibitions; (2) the Hebrew idiom for "one to another" requires a plural verb and named objects, which is not the case here; (3) the Mosaic code "bases its legislation upon the existence of polygamy, and thus authorises it" — citing Exodus 21:9–10, the law of primogeniture in Deuteronomy 21:15–17, and the Levirate law. David, "their best king," took many wives "without reproof," and God gave him more (2 Samuel 12:8). The Jewish interpreters have always understood this as referring to marriage with two sisters simultaneously. The purpose is "to vex her" — the first wife would be roused to jealousy, converting natural sisterly love into enmity, precluding a case like Jacob with Leah and Rachel. "In her lifetime" limits the prohibition: after the first sister dies, a man is at liberty to marry her sister. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch**: The prohibition is against marrying two sisters at the same time — "to pack both together into one marriage bond, and so place the sisters in carnal union through their common husband, and disturb the sisterly relation, as the marriage with two sisters that was forced upon Jacob had evidently done." No punishment is fixed for this. After the death of the first wife, a man was free to marry her sister. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

**Guzik**: The Puritan commentator John Trapp believed this was also a command against polygamy, "but this is not clear from the text itself." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-18/)

**Matthew Henry**: This article "supposes a connivance at polygamy, as some other laws then did (Exodus 21:10; Deuteronomy 21:15), but forbids a man's marrying two sisters, as Jacob did, because between those who had before been equal there would be apt to arise greater jealousies and animosities." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/18.htm)

---

### v. 19: "You must not approach a woman…during her menstrual period"

**Ellicott** notes that this verse continues the prohibitions but shifts from incest to other forms of unchastity. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Keil & Delitzsch**: The prohibition covers both menstruation and after childbirth (the "fountain of bleeding"). Both guilty persons were to be "cut off from their nation" — i.e., punished with death (Leviticus 20:18). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

**Guzik**: This is an echo of Leviticus 15:19–24 where the penalty was ritual washing. There is no specific mention of a marriage relationship — "a woman" includes a wife but goes beyond marriage. In marriage, this was a command for sexual restraint and honor even within the marital relationship. The New Testament counterpart is 1 Corinthians 7:3: "the universal Christian values of servanthood and self-sacrifice demand that a spouse practice restraint of their sexual expectations when love and care for the other would require it." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-18/)

---

### v. 20: "You must not lie carnally with your neighbor's wife"

**Keil & Delitzsch**: The Hebrew literally means "thou shalt not give thy pouring as seed" (make her pregnant), "to defile thyself with her" — a defilement punished as adultery by stoning to death of both parties (Leviticus 20:10; Deuteronomy 22:22; cf. John 8:5). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

**Guzik**: This echoes the seventh commandment (Exodus 20:14). No justification is allowed — not "My partner doesn't understand me" or "we are in love" or "God led us to be with each other." Adultery is "an assault on the nuclear family" (quoting Rooker). It also defiles the person committing it, "showing them to be an unfaithful and uncontrolled person." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-18/)

**Matthew Henry**: This is a law to preserve the honour of the marriage-bed that it should not be "invaded by an adulterer." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/18.htm)

---

### v. 21: "You must not give any of your children to be sacrificed to Molech"

**Keil & Delitzsch**: Moloch (always written with the article in Hebrew) was "an old Canaanitish idol" related to Baal, a sun-god worshipped by child sacrifice. The idol was represented by a brazen statue, hollow and heatable, with a bull's head and arms stretched out to receive children. From Ahaz onward, children were slain at Jerusalem in the valley of Ben-hinnom. However, Keil distinguishes between "passing through the fire" (a februation, or fire-baptism consecrating children to Moloch without actual burning) and later full sacrifice. If Israelites had actually sacrificed children before Ahaz, "the burning would certainly have been mentioned before." This worship was punished by death by stoning (Leviticus 20:3). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

**Guzik**: The horrific worship involved heating a metal statue until red hot, then placing a living infant on its outstretched hands while drums drowned out the screams. Psalm 106:37 identifies Molech with the demonic. Despite this clear command, even Solomon built a temple to Molech (1 Kings 11:7). Guzik notes that many scholars connect Molech worship in this context to infanticide used as "a form of birth control to eliminate children born outside of marriage — the consequence of the very sexual sins God had forbidden." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-18/)

**Precept Austin (MacDonald)**: "According to one tradition there was an opening at the back of the brazen idol, and after a fire was made within it, each parent had to come and with his own hands place his firstborn child in the white-hot, outstretched arms of Molech." Drums were beaten so the baby's cries could not be heard. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_18_commentary)

---

### v. 22: "You must not lie with a man as with a woman; that is an abomination"

**Keil & Delitzsch**: This is the crime of paederastia, "that sin of Sodom (Genesis 19:5), to which the whole of the heathen were more or less addicted (Romans 1:27), and from which even the Israelites did not keep themselves free (Judges 19:22)." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

**Guzik**: "This is a simple and clear command against same-sex sexual acts." God's intention for sexual expression is within the marriage covenant between one man and one woman. He distinguishes between condemning the sexual practice as sin and "treating people with the respect and compassion due to those made in God's image," noting the modern confusion between viewing homosexuality "as an identity versus as a behavior." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-18/)

**Precept Austin**: "God's Word is clear and unequivocal that it is sin (cf. Romans 1:26, 27; 1 Corinthians 6:9, 10)." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_18_commentary)

**Matthew Henry**: "Other sins level men with the beasts, but these sink them much lower. That ever there should have been occasion for the making of these laws…is the perpetual reproach and scandal of human nature; and the giving of men up to these vile affections was frequently the punishment of their idolatries; so the apostle shows, Romans 1:24." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/18.htm)

*Note on denominational differences:* I was unable to retrieve pages from sites representing traditions that differ on the application of v. 22 (e.g., some modern mainline Protestant, Catholic, or Orthodox approaches that may read this verse in light of broader contextual or historical-critical considerations). The sources accessed all represent the traditional/conservative reading. I note this gap in coverage.

---

### v. 23: "You must not lie carnally with any animal…that is a perversion"

**Keil & Delitzsch**: Lying with animals was connected in Egypt with the worship of the goat — at Mendes especially, where "the women lay down before he-goats" (Herodotus 2:46; Strabo 17, p. 802). Aelian relates an account of the crime committed with a dog in Rome. In modern Egypt (per Sonnini), men were said to lie even with female crocodiles. The Hebrew word *tebel* (confusion/perversion) is used here as in v. 15. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

**Guzik**: God's intention for sexual expression is within the marriage covenant between one man and one woman. "Sexual acts with animals do not fulfill this intention. They go against God's design and the ultimate benefit of humanity." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-18/)

**Matthew Henry**: These are "sins not to be named nor thought of without the utmost abhorrence imaginable." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/18.htm)

---

### vv. 24–25: "Do not defile yourselves…Even the land has become defiled…the land will vomit out its inhabitants"

**Keil & Delitzsch**: God points to the fact that the nations He was driving out had defiled the land by such abominations. The preterite verbs ("the land vomited out") are prophetic (cf. Leviticus 20:22–23), and the expression is poetical: "the land is personified as a living creature, which violently rejects food that it dislikes." Keil quotes Cornelius a Lapide: "By this figure Scripture wishes to signify the enormity of the crimes, because the irrational creatures themselves, always obedient to their Creator and fighting for Him, detest such sinners, and the land, as it were, vomits them out when they are expelled from it." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/leviticus-18.html)

**Precept Austin**: "It is no accident that impurity and idolatry are found together in the same chapter. A person's morality is always the fruit of his theology, his concept of God. The Canaanites were a graphic illustration of the degradation that idolatry produces." (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_18_commentary)

**Morgan's Exposition**: This passage contains "a most important declaration, explaining the judgment of God upon the people of these lands. It is that the reason for such judgment is to be found in the practice of these abominations with terrible effects produced upon the peoples, so that they were utterly corrupt." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gcm/leviticus-18.html)

---

### vv. 26–28: "You are to keep My statutes…so if you defile the land, it will vomit you out"

**Guzik**: God's laws apply equally to "your native-born nor the foreigner who lives among you." The warning is that the same judgment that fell on the Canaanites would fall on Israel if they committed the same sins — and indeed, "this was the very reason God had Israelites driven out of the land in the Babylonian captivity." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-18/)

---

### v. 29: "Anyone who commits any of these abominations must be cut off from among his people"

**Precept Austin**: The phrase "cut off" (*karath*) can mean excommunication from the covenant community, premature death, or divine judgment. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_18_commentary)

---

### v. 30: "You must keep My charge…I am the LORD your God"

**Ellicott**: The phrase "I am the LORD your God," which opened the chapter in v. 2 and was repeated in v. 4, closes it here — forming a literary inclusio. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-18.html)

**Matthew Henry**: This is "a sovereign antidote against this infection." He offers three notes: (1) "Sinful customs are abominable customs, and their being common and fashionable does not make them at all the less abominable." (2) "It is of pernicious consequence to admit and allow of any one sinful custom, because one will make way for many. The way of sin is downhill." (3) "A close and constant adherence to God's ordinances is the most effectual preservative from the infection of gross sin." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/leviticus/18.htm)

**Precept Austin**: The chapter structure comes full circle — vv. 1–23 tell them what not to do; vv. 24–30 tell them why. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_18_commentary)
